title: Introduction
focus: the origin of the novel and the idea of creation

teacherSummary.text: Writing in 1831, Shelley explains how the novel began: a rainy summer near Geneva in 1816, a ghost-story contest with Byron and Percy Shelley, conversations about galvanism, and a waking vision of a 'pale student of unhallowed arts' kneeling beside the thing he had put together. She calls the book her 'hideous progeny.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Introduction,” how does Shelley show the origin of the novel and the idea of creation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Introduction, how does Shelley develop the idea of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Introduction develops the idea of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and allusion shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Introduction (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Introduction suggests about the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's point of view and allusion), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses point of view in Introduction to complicate the reader's understanding of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Introduction within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Introduction alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Introduction and its treatment of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's point of view and allusion, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Introduction as evidence for a larger claim about the origin of the novel and the idea of creation in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Introduction as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: I busied myself to think of a story—a story to rival those which had excited us to this task. One which would speak to the mysterious fears of our nature, and awaken thrilling horror—one to make the reader dread to look round, to curdle the blood, and quicken the beatings of the heart. If I did not accomplish these things, my ghost story would be unworthy of its name. I thought and pondered—vainly. I felt that blank incapability of invention which is the greatest misery of authorship, when dull Nothing replies to our anxious invocations. Have you thought of a story? I was asked each morning, and each morning I was forced to reply with a mortifying negative.

literaryElements.label: Point of view
literaryElements.explanation: Shelley speaks in her own voice, thirteen years later, as an author looking back. She shapes a legend about herself: a shy young woman among famous poets who cannot think of a story until a vision comes. Ask students what she gains by presenting the book as a dream rather than a plan.

literaryElements.label: Allusion
literaryElements.explanation: The Introduction is thick with real names (Byron, Percy Shelley, Dr. Darwin, galvanism). Each one ties the fiction to real science and real literary rivalry, which is why the story felt possible to its first readers.

literaryElements.label: Imagery
literaryElements.explanation: The vision is told in sharp visual details: the kneeling student, the "hideous phantasm," the yellow, watery eyes. Students will meet these images again in Chapter V; flag them now.

themesAndDevelopment.development: Shelley calls the book her "hideous progeny" and sends it out into the world, as Victor does his creature; but unlike Victor she wishes it to "prosper." The author models the care the character fails to give.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: the dream
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Dreams recur through the novel (Victor's nightmare after the creation). Here the dream is creative; later it becomes a punishment.

evidence.quote: I saw the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together
evidence.use: "Unhallowed" means unholy, and "thing" refuses the creation a name. Students can use this to argue that the novel judges the act of creation as a transgression from its first image.

evidence.quote: And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper
evidence.use: Shelley presents herself as a parent of the book. Use this to connect author and character: both make something "hideous," but only one blesses it.

evidence.quote: Invention, it must be humbly admitted, does not consist in creating out of void, but out of chaos
evidence.use: Shelley's theory of creativity: you build from existing materials, as Victor builds from old bones. Good evidence for a claim about the novel's self-awareness.

claimEvidenceReasoning.claim: Shelley frames her novel as a creation that, unlike Victor's, is accepted and sent out with care.
claimEvidenceReasoning.evidence: And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper
claimEvidenceReasoning.reasoning: By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make.

weDoAnswers: "Hideous" admits the book is frightening; "progeny" (offspring) makes her its mother; "prosper" is a parent's blessing. Link: Victor makes a creature but never blesses it, so the line sets up the theme of responsibility.
facilitation: If students say the Introduction "is just background," ask why Shelley added it in 1831: how does knowing a nineteen-year-old dreamed this change how we read the book?
Expect a split on whether the dream story is literally true. Use the teacher-notes flag: it is her later recollection, and that is itself a choice.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the chapter for point of view, allusion (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this chapter suggest about the origin of the novel and the idea of creation? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Introduction develops the idea of the origin of the novel and the idea of creation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and allusion shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Shelley frames her novel as a creation that, unlike Victor's, is accepted and sent out with care. When the text says “And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper” (Introduction, paragraph 15), it shows this directly. By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Shelley frames her novel as a creation that, unlike Victor's, is accepted and sent out with care. Useful evidence: “I saw the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together” (Introduction, paragraph 11): "Unhallowed" means unholy, and "thing" refuses the creation a name. Students can use this to argue that the novel judges the act of creation as a transgression from its first image. On allusion: The Introduction is thick with real names (Byron, Percy Shelley, Dr. Darwin, galvanism). Each one ties the fiction to real science and real literary rivalry, which is why the story felt possible to its first readers. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
